title: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: the BTS 2023 pathway

guidelineVersions: BTS Clinical Statement on pleural procedures (Thorax 2023)

related.why: Tension pneumothorax in the trauma primary survey
Other causes of acute breathlessness in surgical patients

brief.role: Core surgical trainee covering thoracic surgery
brief.scenario: Mr Liam Stewart, 22, developed sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness six hours ago while sitting at his desk. He smokes. He has no lung disease. Written findings: a PA chest X-ray shows a fine, sharp white line following the curve of the left lung, with a 3 cm rim between the lung edge and the chest wall at the level of the hilum, with no lung markings between this line and the chest wall. The trachea and mediastinum are central. There is no fluid level. The lung inside the line and the right lung look normal.
brief.task: Interpret the written chest X-ray findings and answer the examiner's questions on his management and advice.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Read the findings, check for high-risk features, then let his symptoms and priorities choose the treatment.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Deciding on a chest drain by size alone.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Before I interpret the X-ray: is he stable, and how short of breath is he?"

grid.label: Interpret the X-ray findings
grid.fail: Misses the pneumothorax, or calls tension from the X-ray alone.
grid.pass: Left pneumothorax: visible visceral pleural edge, no lung markings beyond it; notes the trachea and mediastinum are central.
grid.high: Also checks for a fluid level (haemopneumothorax), underlying lung disease and the other side; knows a skin fold can mimic the edge.

grid.label: High-risk features
grid.fail: Does not look for features that mandate intervention.
grid.pass: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Checks BTS high-risk features: haemodynamic compromise, significant hypoxia, bilateral, lung disease, age 50 or over with smoking, haemopneumothorax.
grid.high: States any high-risk feature means intervention (usually a drain) regardless of preference; secondary pneumothorax needs inpatient review.

grid.label: Symptoms and size
grid.fail: Uses size alone: small means home, large means drain.
grid.pass: Symptoms decide whether to intervene; size decides whether it is safe (usually 2 cm or more laterally or apically on the X-ray).
grid.high: Knows conservative care suits minimal symptoms regardless of size; if too small to intervene safely but high-risk, get a CT.

grid.label: Choose with the patient
grid.fail: Inserts a drain without discussing options.
grid.pass: Asks his priority: avoid a procedure (conservative, outpatient review), or rapid relief (ambulatory device or needle aspiration); drain if aspiration fails.
grid.high: Gives the review plan: conservative review every 2–4 days; aspiration success is improved symptoms and film; clinic follow-up at 2–4 weeks.

grid.label: Procedure safety
grid.fail: Cannot describe the safe triangle, or plans a posterior or low site.
grid.pass: Safe triangle: lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, line at nipple level (fifth intercostal space), apex below the axilla.
grid.high: Inserts just above a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle under the rib above; avoids a posterior approach.

grid.label: Recognise tension
grid.fail: Waits for a chest X-ray in a hypotensive, hypoxic patient.
grid.pass: Tension is clinical: immediate decompression (needle or open thoracostomy), then a chest drain.
grid.high: Adds that tension at the first episode is a reason to consider surgery to prevent recurrence.

grid.label: Discharge advice
grid.fail: Tells him he can fly or dive next week.
grid.pass: Return at once if breathless; no flying until the film shows resolution, then wait 7 days; stop smoking; follow-up X-ray.
grid.high: Recurrence about 1 in 3; diving discouraged permanently unless surgical pleurectomy; surgery after a second ipsilateral or first contralateral episode.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Here are the findings on his chest X-ray.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Left pneumothorax, trachea central. No fluid level, so no haemopneumothorax; the lung looks normal and the right side is clear. That's a true pleural edge, not a skin fold.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He's now breathless and hypoxic at rest.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's a high-risk feature, so he needs intervention, usually a drain, whatever his preference.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Suppose it were a 1 cm apical rim.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If he's barely symptomatic, conservative care is fine at any size. If he's high-risk and it's too small to intervene safely, I'd get a CT to find a window.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Review every 2 to 4 days as an outpatient, and a drain if it enlarges. After aspiration, success means better symptoms and a better film. Clinic at 2 to 4 weeks.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd go just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle, and avoid a posterior approach.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: And if he'd presented with tension?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Decompress and drain, then consider surgery, because tension at a first episode is a reason to prevent recurrence.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: About 1 in 3 recur. Diving is off permanently unless he has a surgical pleurectomy. I'd offer surgery after a second ipsilateral or first contralateral episode.

failures.move: Choosing a drain by size alone.
failures.consequence: An avoidable procedure for a minimally symptomatic patient.
A hypoxic or older smoker is sent home for conservative care.

failures.move: Waiting for an X-ray in suspected tension.

failures.consequence: Recurrence at altitude or depth, far from help.

recovery.line: It depends on his symptoms, high-risk features and priorities; size tells me whether intervention is safe.
Symptomatic? High-risk? Safe to intervene? Then what matters most to him.

knowledge.fact: BTS 2023: conservative care can be considered for minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax regardless of size.
Sufficient size to intervene: usually 2 cm or more laterally or apically, or any size on CT with a safe window.
Recurrence after a first primary pneumothorax: 32%.
Fly 7 days after radiological resolution; scuba diving discouraged permanently unless surgical pleurectomy.
Safe triangle: pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, fifth intercostal space, apex below the axilla.

recall.think: Tension kills; a high-risk patient sent home can deteriorate.
recall.say: "Primary spontaneous pneumothorax, no high-risk features: management depends on his symptoms and priorities."
do: Drain if aspiration fails or high-risk

numbers.meaning: usual size needed to intervene safely
wait after radiological resolution before flying

recall.trap: A large pneumothorax in a comfortable patient does not need a drain.
recall.finish: Clinic follow-up at 2–4 weeks; surgery for a second ipsilateral or first contralateral episode.

curveballs.prompt: BP 80/50, SpO2 84%, trachea deviated to the right.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Tension: decompress immediately, then chest drain; do not wait for imaging.

curveballs.prompt: He is 64 with COPD and the same X-ray findings.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Secondary pneumothorax, high risk: admit and drain.

curveballs.prompt: Needle aspiration leaves him still breathless with little change on the film.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Aspiration has failed: insert a chest drain.
